kjv: it (the sword) contemneth the rod of my son, [as] every tree (KJV 21:10)
mine: You have despised the rod, my son, with everything of wood
note: The Hebrew shevet beni moeset kol-ets ("rod of my son, despising every tree") is one of the most obscure lines in Ezekiel; both renderings are guesses at a probably damaged text.

kjv: he (the king of Babylon) made [his] arrows bright, he consulted with images (KJV 21:21)
mine: He (the king of Babylon) shakes the arrows; he consults the teraphim
note: qilqal bahitsim means "shook" the arrows (belomancy, drawing lots from a quiver), not polishing them; terafim are household cult figures, a specific object rather than generic "images".
mitsnefet is the turban of the high priest (Exod 28:4), pointing to removal of both priestly and royal insignia; "diadem" loses the priestly reference.

kjv: until he come whose right it is (KJV 21:27)
mine: until he comes, the one to whom judgment belongs
note: asher-lo hammishpat: mishpat is "judgment/justice", and in context it may be Nebuchadnezzar who is given the judging task; KJV's "right" (and its messianic echo of Gen 49:10) is one possible reading. Context: literal 'the one to whom judgment belongs'; referent left open (low confidence). Mishpat can mean 'judgment' or 'right, due' (Deut 21:17; Jer 32:8), and the line echoes Gen 49:10. It may mean Nebuchadnezzar, to whom God commits judgment (cf. 23:24), or the rightful Davidic king for whom the crown waits (cf. 34:23-24; 37:24). The LXX and most versions take 'right'. The literal English leaves both open. Other possible meanings: (1) 'until he comes whose right it is' — the rightful (messianic) king; LXX 'to whom it belongs', KJV, NASB, NRSV, NIV, NJPS, much Jewish and Christian exegesis; (2) 'the one to whom I have assigned the judgment' — Babylon's king as God's agent; NET, W. L. Moran and many commentators.
